messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At sixty-eight, Rajesh’s life had narrowed to a careful negotiation with a past he could no longer name. The assault itself had occurred in a stifling, windowless corridor behind a municipal warehouse, where a stranger’s hands had pinned him against cold concrete and the heavy, wet sounds of the attack had completely drowned out his own panicked breathing. He had survived it, but he could never find words to describe what he endured; the memory remained locked in his body, resurfacing as a sharp, familiar pain in his ribs and shoulders whenever the past threatened to intrude. Knowing what had happened to him did not bring clarity, only a crushing sense that his reactions since the event proved he was a lousy coper. This conviction that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, combined with the belief that he was permanently an outsider, fundamentally altered how he navigated the world. Because he viewed himself through this lens of permanent failure, his awareness of potential danger sharpened into a constant, exhausting alertness. He became hyper-vigilant to any sudden or loud noises, treating every unexpected sound as a direct threat to his safety. This perceived threat quickly dictated his daily routines. He could no longer tolerate being alone in a room or building, finding empty spaces more dangerous than crowded ones. To manage the rising panic, he always sat with his back against a wall so he could watch the room, a posture that kept his muscles corded in preparation for flight. When he worked at the downtown non-profit, navigating shared administrative halls to file grant reports, the sudden brush of a colleague’s shoulder would trigger a violent startle to touch, his heart hammering as he instinctively recoiled. The physical jolt of that reaction confirmed his deepest fear that he was broken beyond repair, which in turn pulled the auditory echoes of the assault back into his mind with renewed force. The remembered sounds and the return of that familiar pain would spike his threat monitoring to a fever pitch, making him listen intently for any sound that might mean someone was entering his home. To dampen the overwhelming feelings that threatened to drown him, Rajesh began to hurt himself physically, pressing his knuckles into his desk or biting his lip until it bled. Yet these attempts to release the tension only anchored the traumatic memories more firmly; the sting of the self-inflicted pain would immediately trigger another wave of auditory recall, proving to him that his coping strategies were failing. This failure reinforced his negative appraisals, convincing him that he would never feel normal again and permanently cemented his status as an outsider. The cycle tightened with every passing week: his avoidance and self-harm bred more memories, which fueled more threat monitoring, which only deepened his sense of incompetence. By the time he walked into the clinic, the exhaustion of maintaining a perpetual perimeter had made it impossible to continue his work. He sought help because he was terrified that the loop was closing completely, and what he hoped for was simply a way to quiet the internal alarm long enough to exist without bracing for the next attack.
